name: cpp-sort
listed_description: Sorting algorithms & related tools for C++14.
reason: Directional claims only on reachable pages; the numbers sit in imgur graph images (i.imgur.com blocked by egress). The wiki Benchmarks page (g++ 16.2 -O3 -march=native -std=c++26 on EndeavourOS, or MinGW-w64 g++ 12.0 -O3 on Windows 10, double elements, scripts in the repo benchmarks folder) says only that ska_sort 'is almost always the fastest', 'ska_sort beats all the other algorithms on average' and 'libstdc++ std::sort doesn't adapt well to patterns meant to defeat median-of-3 quicksort', with no figures. The README graph compares heap_sort adapters against each other, not std::sort. The Sorters, Changelog and releases pages hold no std::sort or std::stable_sort ratio; a web search returned 'std::sort 9.04, pdqsort 4.65, ska_sort 2.00' but those numbers come from the Boost.Sort mailing-list ska_sort post, not from cpp-sort, and that page is blocked. Retry from an environment that can open the wiki's imgur graphs (https://github.com/Morwenn/cpp-sort/wiki/Benchmarks); the benchmark scripts are public, so a tier A record is likely once the graphs are readable.

name: cppcodec
listed_description: Header-only C++11 library to encode/decode base64, base32 and hex with consistent, flexible API.
reason: Not claimed faster. README 'Philosophy and trade-offs' says good performance is a goal but not the top priority and that 'on release builds, depending on the C++ compiler, cppcodec runs in between (approx.) 100% and 300% of time compared to "regular" optimized base64 implementations', beaten by vectorised (aklomp/base64) and large-table (Chrome) implementations. test/benchmark_cppcodec.cpp times cppcodec's own codecs only (hex_lower, base32_rfc4648, base64_rfc4648) with no baseline, and the guessed protobuf baseline is a different job. No third-party shootout including cppcodec was reachable.

name: cproc
listed_description: A C11 compiler using QBE as a backend. [ISC]
reason: git.sr.ht is blocked by egress; the README read through the GitHub mirror (michaelforney/cproc) makes no speed claim (goals are C standard conformance and building real software). The only number found, from a WebSearch snippet of Brian Callahan's 2021-10-10 blog post (briancallahan.net/blog/20211010.html, blocked), says code produced with cproc/QBE runs at about 74%-82% of gcc, i.e. slower than the baseline, and gives no compile-time comparison. No faster-than-baseline number exists.

name: Cranium
listed_description: Portable, header-only ANN library in C99. [MIT]
reason: Directional claim only. README says it 'should be reasonably fast as it uses a matrix-based approach' and offers optional CBLAS sgemm; the repo (docs, src, tests) has no benchmark and no comparison with any other library. The docs site 100.github.io/Cranium is blocked by egress but is API documentation.

name: cxx-prettyprint
listed_description: A pretty printing library for C++ containers.
reason: No performance claim at all: the repo (prettyprint.hpp, prettyprint98.hpp, ppdemo*.cpp, README, prettyprint.tex) is a stream-formatting helper, and its README mentions only usage, compile flags and licence. No comparison against printf, snprintf or any other printer anywhere reachable; the project website (louisdx.github.com/cxx-prettyprint) is blocked by egress but is documentation of the output format.
